title: Printed flannel with chevrons
lede: A surviving swatch of Varvara Stepanova’s geometric flannel print, made when constructivist artists turned to designing textiles for Soviet factories.
summary: Wine-red and olive-brown interlocking chevrons on a natural cotton ground. Varvara Stepanova, 1924, V&A.

evidence.note: Viewed the V&A photograph of the swatch T.213-2016 (1600 × 1443 px through the museum’s IIIF service) in a scratch folder. No image is stored.

styles.note: Partial fit: a productivist textile from the constructivist circle. It shares the flat, repeated geometry and diagonal movement, but it uses two muted hues instead of red and black and has no type.

context: The V&A describes the swatch as printed cotton flannel, about 22 × 23–25 cm, “with geometric design of wine red and dull olive-brown chevrons on a pale fawn natural colour ground”, made in Russia in 1924. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1371413/).

After an official appeal in 1923, Stepanova, Popova, and Rodchenko designed prints for the Soviet textile industry. The V&A notes that rural buyers preferred floral prints, so surviving samples are rare. Stepanova’s grandson Alexander Lavrentiev gave the swatch to the V&A director Martin Roth in 2014. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1371413/).
observed: Rows of chevrons point alternately up and down, in a wine red and an olive green-brown.
Pale bands of the unprinted ground run on two diagonals between the chevrons, so the pattern reads as a lattice of zigzags.
The edges are cut and slightly frayed; the flannel nap softens the edges of the print.
interpretation: The swatch shows the style’s diagonal energy transferred to an all-over repeat. The color is quieter than in the posters, which suggests that the red-and-black rule belongs to print, not to every constructivist medium.
Compare [Popova’s design with stars in circles](ref:popova-stars-in-circles-textile-design), which keeps red and black.
borrow: Build a background pattern from two interlocking chevrons and let the gaps between them form a diagonal lattice.
Use a muted red with an earthy second color for a quieter version of the style.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Stepanova died in 1958, so her designs are protected in Russia until the end of 2028 or later (life + 70, plus 4 years if she worked during the Great Patriotic War). The V&A image is shown under the museum’s own terms.
